PARLIAMENT VS STATE LEGISLATURE
THEME ANALYSIS PYQ pattern for this chapter
1. REPEATS

#### A. Presiding Officers
- The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker and goes by a majority of all the then members [2012, 2025]
- On dissolution the Speaker stays till the new House meets, unlike a State Assembly Speaker [2018, 2025]
- Under Art 96 a Speaker facing removal may speak and vote, yet shall not preside [2024]
- The Deputy Speaker is elected on a date the Speaker fixes, bound by no convention [2022]
- The Rajya Sabha Chairman comes from outside the House, the Council Chairman from within [2013]

#### B. Composition and Membership
- A Legislative Council is capped at one third of the Assembly and floored at 40 [2015]
- Qualifications under Art 84 and Art 173, disqualification under Art 103 and Art 192
- Office of profit, the Leader of the Opposition, and Union Territory representation

#### C. Lok Sabha versus Rajya Sabha
- Only the Lok Sabha carries a no confidence motion; Emergency approval and impeachment are shared [2022]
- The Rajya Sabha acts alone under Art 249 and Art 312 [2012]
- Ministers answer collectively to the Lok Sabha under Art 75(3) [2022]

#### D. Privileges and Anti Defection
- Art 105 and Art 194 privileges stay uncodified, the bribery immunity now withdrawn
- Tenth Schedule grounds and exceptions, decided by the presiding officer
- Also tested: prorogation and dissolution [2024], sessions [2020], the Governor's address and State Assembly rules

resolution [2016]

- 2012 to 2016: single answer and two statement sets on Rajya Sabha powers and Councils [2012, 2013, 2015, 2016]
- 2018 to 2022: code sets on presiding officers, sessions and exclusive powers [2018, 2019, 2020, 2022]
- 2024 to 2025: three statement sets on the Speaker and on prorogation [2024, 2025]

DETAILED NOTES
Types of Majority in Parliament
1. Simple (functional/working) majority - more than half of the members present and voting.
– This is the default rule under Art 100(1) and is used for ordinary bills, money bills, confidence and no-confidence motions, censure and adjournment motions, and approval of
proclamations under Arts 356 and 360.
2. Absolute majority - more than half of the total membership of the House (e.g. 272 of 543 in the Lok Sabha). In Lok Sabha (545 seats), 273 seats are required for absolute majority.
– It is not by itself prescribed for any parliamentary decision; it matters chiefly in government formation after a general election.
3. Effective majority - more than half of the effective strength, i.e. total membership minus vacancies ('all the then members').
– Used to remove the Deputy Chairman and Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Arts 90(c), 67(b)) and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Arts 94(c), 96).
4. Special majority - 4 different forms:
(i) Special majority 1: majority of total membership of each House + not less than two thirds of members present and voting
– Constitutional Amendment (Art 368(2))
– Removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges (Art 124(4), Art 217(1)(b))
– Removal of CEC (Art 324(5)) and CAG (Art 148(1)), on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge
– Approval of a National Emergency (Art 352(6))
(ii) Special majority 2: not less than two thirds of the total membership of each House
Impeachment of the President (Art 61)
(iii) Special majority 3: not less than two thirds of members present and voting in the Rajya Sabha
– Parliament legislating on a State List subject in the national interest (Art 249)
– Creating a new All India Service (Art 312)
– Note: These are the two exclusive powers of the Rajya Sabha. It alone holds them because it is the Council of States, so the States must first agree before the Union moves into
their domain.
(iv) Special majority + State ratification
Federal provisions under the Art 368(2) need the special majority in (i) + at least half the States ratify by simple majority

Not a discretionary power in normal circumstances. It is used in two situations:
(a) Private Members' Bills;
(b) Government Bills where the Cabinet resigns after the Bill is passed but before assent, and the new Cabinet advises the
President to withhold assent.
Classic instance: the PEPSU Appropriation Bill, 1954.
Logic: assent is given on aid and advice. Advice from a Council of Ministers that has lost the confidence of the House cannot
bind its successor.
State Bills and Art 304(b)
Bills imposing reasonable restrictions on the freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse within a State can be introduced in
a State Legislature only with the prior sanction of the President. The requirement exists to protect the economic unity of India
under Art 301, by ensuring that a State cannot erect internal trade barriers without a central check on reasonableness.
Reservation of State Bills for the President
The Governor may reserve any Bill for the consideration of the President under Art 200.
(a) Compulsory: where the Bill derogates from the powers of the High Court and endangers its constitutional position.
(b) Needed for protection: a State law on acquisition of estates and property must get the President's assent to be
protected by Art 31A and Art 31C.
If the President returns such a Bill, the State Legislature must reconsider it within 6 months. Even when it comes back, the
President is not obliged to assent.
Why: the quasi federal design lets the Union supervise State laws that touch the judiciary or the federal economic order.
Current constitutional position on assent timelines
April 2025, State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu: a two judge Bench used Art 142 to prescribe timelines and
granted deemed assent to ten pending State Bills.
13 May 2025: President Droupadi Murmu referred 14 questions to the Supreme Court under Art 143(1), noting that Art 200
and Art 201 prescribe no deadlines.
20 November 2025, Special Reference No. 1 of 2025 (five judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI B.R. Gavai) held:
(a) no judicially imposed timeline can bind the Governor (Art 200) or the President (Art 201);
(b) deemed assent has no constitutional basis and cannot be created through Art 142;
(c) the President need not seek the Court's opinion under Art 143 for every reserved Bill;
(d) judicial review survives only for malafide or wholly inert conduct.
Why: separation of powers. A court cannot supply a deadline the framers deliberately left out, or take the place of a
constitutional authority in the legislative chain.
(Source: Supreme Court of India, Special Reference No. 1 of 2025, 2025 INSC 1333)
Money Bill certification under judicial scrutiny
Puttaswamy (2018): the Speaker's Money Bill certificate under Art 110(4) is subject to judicial review.
Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019): whether the Aadhaar Act, 2016 was rightly certified as a Money Bill was referred
to a larger Bench, where it remains pending.
Why it matters: a Money Bill shuts out the Rajya Sabha. So a wrong label is not a procedural slip; it removes one House from
lawmaking.
Joint sittings held so far
Only three joint sittings so far: 1961: Dowry Prohibition Bill; 1978: Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill; 2002: Prevention
of Terrorism Bill.
The rarity shows the mechanism works mainly as a deterrent that pushes the Houses to compromise, not as an ordinary route
to enactment.

1. Consolidated Fund of India (Art 266(1)): Receives all revenues, loans raised (treasury bills, loans, ways and means
advances) and loan repayments. No withdrawal without parliamentary appropriation (Art 114(3)).
2. Contingency Fund of India (Art 267): Placed at the President’s disposal, operated by the Finance Secretary on his
behalf. An imprest for unforeseen expenditure, recouped once Parliament votes a supplementary grant. Corpus
raised from ₹500 crore to ₹30,000 crore by the Finance Act, 2021.
3. Public Account of India (Art 266(2)): Holds money the government keeps as banker or trustee, not owner:
provident funds, small savings, deposits, remittances. Withdrawals by executive action; no parliamentary
appropriation needed (often inverted in questions).

Grants other than the annual grant: Art 115 and Art 116

#### A. Art 115: Supplementary, Additional and Excess Grants
1. Supplementary Grant: When the amount sanctioned for a service in the current year proves insufficient.
2. Additional Grant: For new expenditure on a new service not included in that year’s Budget.
3. Excess Grant: When money already spent exceeds the grant in a past year; voted after the year ends, only after
Public Accounts Committee approval. The only grant regularised retrospectively.

#### B. Art 116: Exceptional Grants
4. Vote on Account: Advance from the Consolidated Fund for part of the year until the Appropriation Bill passes; usually for
two months (longer in election years).
5. Vote of Credit: For unexpected demands too large or uncertain to detail, like a national emergency; effectively a blank
cheque.
6. Exceptional Grant: For a special purpose outside the normal services of any year.

#### C. Token Grant (by practice, not in the Constitution)
7. When new expenditure can be met by reappropriating savings within an existing grant, a token sum of ₹1 is voted just to
secure Parliament’s approval.

Budget stages and parliamentary control over public finance [PRELIMS 2012]
1. The Union Budget passes through six stages:
(a) Presentation of the Annual Financial Statement.
(b) General discussion in both Houses, with no motion and no vote.
(c) Scrutiny by the Departmentally Related Standing Committees.
(d) Voting on Demands for Grants, in the Lok Sabha alone. Cut motions (Disapproval of Policy, Economy, Token) may be
moved; undiscussed Demands are put to vote together under the guillotine.
(e) Passing of the Appropriation Bill (Art 114).
(f) Passing of the Finance Bill, which gives effect to the tax proposals. Its declared provisions take effect at once under
the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, but lapse if the Bill is not passed within 75 days.
2. Article 116 provides the interim devices: a Vote on Account, an advance grant from the Consolidated Fund to meet
expenditure for a part of the financial year pending the passing of the Appropriation Act, together with votes of credit
and exceptional grants.
3. Article 115 provides for supplementary, additional and excess grants, excess grants being examined first by the Public
Accounts Committee.
4. Post-budgetary control runs through the Comptroller and Auditor General under Article 148 and the financial
committees.
5. India has no Parliamentary Budget Office, so a periodic or mid-year review of programmes against macroeconomic
forecasts by such a body is not a mode of parliamentary control here.
The three readings: stages an Ordinary Bill passes through in each House
1. First Reading (Introduction)
- Mover seeks leave to introduce; if opposed, brief statements from both sides, then the question is put.
- Introduction + publication in the Gazette completes it.
- If published before introduction, no leave is needed.
2. Second Reading (Most important stage)
- Stage 1, General discussion on the Bill’s principles; the House may:
- take it into consideration at once,
- refer it to a Select Committee of that House,
- refer it to a Joint Committee of both Houses (with the other House’s concurrence), or
- circulate it for public opinion.
- The presiding officer may also refer it to a Departmentally Related Standing Committee, whose report is advisory.
- Stage 2, Clause-by-clause consideration: Amendments are moved and voted; the core of Parliament’s influence on
legislation.
3. Third Reading (Passage)
- Debate limited to accepting or rejecting the Bill as a whole.
- Only formal, verbal or consequential amendments allowed; passed by the required majority.
Final Step: Sent to the other House for all three stages, then for President’s assent under Art 111.

A Parliamentary Committee is a body of MPs that:
1. Is appointed or elected by the House, or nominated by the Speaker/Chairman;
2. Works under the direction of the Speaker/Chairman;
3. Presents its report to the House or the presiding officer;
4. Has a secretariat provided by the Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha Secretariat.
Why needed: Parliament has limited time and large, technical business. Committees allow detailed scrutiny, expert
evidence, and bipartisan discussion away from the floor, which is why they are called “mini-Parliaments”.
Constitutional basis: The Constitution does not list specific committees. They are created under the Rules of Procedure
framed under Art 118, with privileges flowing from Art 105 (Parliament) and Art 194 (States).
Consultative Committees are not Parliamentary Committees, since they do not meet all four conditions above.

Reasons for Adoption
1. Familiarity with the System: India's established parliamentary traditions over the past decades,
particularly after the Government of India Act, 1935.
2. Preference for Responsibility
3. Harmony Between Legislature and Executive: to avoid conflicts between the legislature and the
executive, common in the U.S. presidential system.
4. Nature of Indian Society: India's diverse and complex society
5. Flexibility: allows for power-sharing arrangements and coalition governments, crucial for a diverse
country like India.
Features of the Parliamentary system
1. Nominal and Real Executive
2. Collective Responsibility to the Lok
Sabha (Article 75(3)).
3. Political Homogeneity - Ministers
usually belong to the same political party
or coalition.
4. Membership of Legislature
5. Leadership of the Prime Minister as the
head of government and leader of the
majority party.
6. Dissolution of Lower House
7. Opposition and Accountability - Existence of a responsible opposition ensures continuous legislative
scrutiny.
Functions of Parliament:
1. Legislative Function
a. Makes laws on subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists (Article 245-246).
b. Can create new states, alter boundaries, and legislate on State List (Article 249).
2. Judicial Function- Impeaches the President (Article 61), removal of judges of the Supreme Court/High
Courts, and punishes for contempt or breach of privilege.
3. Deliberative Function - Serves as a forum for national debate on policies, bills, and public issues,
ensuring democratic deliberation.
4. Constitutional Function - Amends the Constitution under Article 368 through special majority
procedures.
a. Financial Function
b. Exercises control over national finances - passes the Budget, Demands for Grants, and Appropriation
Bills.
c. Enforces financial accountability through the Public Accounts Committee and Estimates Committee.
5. Executive Control and Oversight
a. Holds the Council of Ministers accountable through questions, debates, adjournment motions, and
no-confidence motions (Article 75(3)).
b. Approves President's ordinances and emergency proclamations.
6. Electoral Function
a. Participates in the election of the President and Vice-President.
b. Elects the Deputy Speaker, Deputy Chairman, and committee members.

Parliamentary Sovereignty:
The Doctrine of Parliamentary Sovereignty means that Parliament holds the supreme power within the
State, with no legal limitations on its authority or jurisdiction. In India, however, there is constitutional
sovereignty, not parliamentary sovereignty.
Limitations on Parliamentary Sovereignty in India
1. The written Constitution defines and limits the powers of Parliament.
2. Supremacy of the Constitution - Any law violating the Constitution can be declared void by courts
under Article 13.
3. Judicial Review guaranteed under Articles 13, 32, and 226.
4. Separation of powers: Eg. Articles 121 and 211 prohibit legislative discussions on the conduct of Supreme
Court and High Court judges.
5. Basic Structure Doctrine - Parliament cannot destroy or damage the basic features like democracy,
secularism, federalism, rule of law, and judicial independence.
6. Federal Structure of Governance - States have exclusive jurisdiction over matters in the State List
(Seventh Schedule), unless under extraordinary provisions.
7. Limited Amendment Procedure - Some constitutional amendments require ratification by at least half
of the states (Article 368(2)). Eg. Amendments affecting High Court jurisdictions.
8. International Law and Treaties - Eg. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) - SC used CEDAW (Convention
on Elimination of Discrimination Against Women) to frame guidelines.
9. Presidential Veto Limitations: Eg. pocket veto
Mechanisms available with the Indian Parliament to ensure executive accountability:
1. Question Hour - MPs question ministers on policy and governance issues.
2. Zero Hour - Members raise urgent issues without notice. Eg. Manipur violence (2023) and train
accidents.
3. Motion of No-Confidence (Article 75(3)) - If passed, the government must resign. Eg. No-confidence
motion (2023) on Manipur issue
4. Censure and Adjournment Motions - Used to express disapproval of executive policies. Eg. Censure
motion (2012) against FDI in retail policy.
5. Cut Motions on Demands for Grants - Allow Parliament to reduce or reject specific budget allocations.
6. Parliamentary Committees - PAC, Estimates, and Standing Committees ensure financial and policy
oversight. Eg. PAC (2011) report on 2G spectrum case.
7. Calling Attention and Half-Hour Discussions - Seek ministerial statements on urgent matters.
8. Discussion on Presidential Address - Enables MPs to review government priorities
9. Privilege Motions - Raised when ministers mislead Parliament.
10. Approval of Ordinances and Emergencies - Eg. Farm laws (2020)
Role of Rajya Sabha
Rajya Sabha is the second chamber of the parliament and consists of the representatives of the States and the
Union Territories and persons nominated by the President of India.
Jawaharlal Nehru: "The Rajya Sabha represents the voice of reason and sobriety in our democracy."
G.V. Mavalankar: "A second chamber is not a luxury in a federal system; it is a necessity for balanced
legislation."

### [Smash Mains Source Page 120](pages/mains/mains_page_120.pdf)

Powers of Rajya Sabha
Equal Powers with Lok Sabha
1. Ordinary Bills: can approve, reject, or suggest amendments to ordinary bills.
2. Constitutional Amendments: require a two-thirds majority in each house.
3. Impeachment of the President: Can initiate and participate
4. Proclamation of Emergency: Must approve the proclamation of National Emergency, President's Rule,
and Financial Emergency within a specified period.
Special Powers of Rajya Sabha:
1. Article 249: authorize Parliament to pass laws on state list subject, in the national interest.
2. Article 312: RS can authorise the Parliament to create new All-India Services.
3. Removal of Vice President: RS alone can initiate a move for the removal of the VP.
Limited Powers w.r.t Lok Sabha:
1. No-Confidence Motion: It cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha.
2. Money bills: return bill to LS within 14 days, LS can either accept or reject
3. Joint Sitting: Speaker of LS presides and Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha govern.
Relevance of the Rajya Sabha in Indian Democracy
1. Permanent and Continuous Chamber (Article 83) - ensures continuity in polity.
2. Revisory and Deliberative Role
a. Acts as a "House of revision", ensuring in-depth scrutiny of Bills passed by the LS.
b. Checks hasty or populist legislation, enhancing legislative quality.
c. Provides a platform for smaller and regional parties to articulate their views.
3. Voice of the States (Articles 80 & 81) - Functions as a federal bridge, giving states a voice in national
law-making and promoting cooperative federalism.
4. Constitutional and Electoral Role - Plays a key role in constitutional amendments (Article 368) and
election of the President and Vice-President.
1. President nominates 12 eminent members, enhancing diversity and expertise, bringing non-political
and intellectual voices into national discourse.
Concerns Related to Rajya Sabha:
Legislative Role
1. Bypassing through Money Bill Route - Eg. Aadhaar Act, 2016.
2. Accusations of Obstructionism - Eg. delaying "progressive" legislation, such as the Privy Purses Bill
(1970), Panchayati Raj Bills (1989).
3. Declining Productivity - Productivity fell from 95% (1990s) to 74% (2014-21), with a low of 40% in
2018, due to frequent disruptions and walkouts.
Executive Accountability Role
1. Rajya Sabha cannot move a no-confidence motion, limiting direct executive accountability.
2. Limited Role in Financial Oversight - no representation in the Estimates Committee and a restricted
role in PAC.
3. Political Partisanship - Increasing party polarization has led to deadlocks and reduced its deliberative
character.
Representative Role
1. Dilution of Federal Character - 2003 Amendment to RPA and Kuldip Nayar judgment removed the
domicile requirement, weakening state representation.
122

### [Smash Mains Source Page 121](pages/mains/mains_page_121.pdf)

2. Unequal Representation of States in Rajya Sabha - Eg. Uttar Pradesh (31 seats) has more representation
than all N-E states combined.
3. A 'Parking Lot' for Wealthy Candidates - 36% of current RS members have criminal antecedents and
87% have assets over INR 1 crore, with 12% billionaires (ADR).
4. Misuse of Presidential Nominations: used as a tool for "political rehabilitation" of party loyalists.
Way Forward:
1. Equal representation for each state, so that large states do not dominate the proceedings. (US system)
2. NCRWC, 2002 - Called for a clear procedure for nominating eminent members
3. Punchhi Commission (2010)- expanding the electoral college for Rajya Sabha to include panchayats
and municipalities.
4. Procedural and Institutional Reforms - Allow Rajya Sabha sessions independent of Lok Sabha to
underline its permanent and continuous nature.
5. Enhance legislative research and committee resources to support members.
With the Planning Commission abolished and the Inter-State Council inactive, Rajya Sabha should serve as
a permanent institutional bridge for federal consultation.
X-Factor Pointers
- At present, 79 Parliaments of the world (41% of the total number) are bicameral.
- In The Federalist, the famous essays written in 1787-88 by James Madison, Alexander Hamilton and
John Jay, it was stated that the second chamber enables a second and reflective expression of
representative opinion besides checking the propensity to yield to the impulse of sudden and violent
passions.
Role of Presiding officer
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Article 93) and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) are the
Presiding Officers of the two Houses of Parliament.
They are entrusted with maintaining order, ensuring legislative discipline, and upholding the dignity and
autonomy of Parliament.
Functions:
Legislative Functions
1. Presides over sittings and ensures orderly conduct of business and debates.
2. Decides on admissibility of questions, motions, and resolutions.
3. Certifies Bills as Money Bills (Article 110) - a decision that is final and binding.
Disciplinary Role -
Maintains decorum and order in the House; can suspend or name members for disorderly conduct.
Quasi-Judicial Functions -
Decides questions of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law).
Administrative and Procedural Role
1. Interprets rules of procedure and parliamentary practices.
2. Allocates time for debates and discussions, and decides the agenda of the House.
123

### [Smash Mains Source Page 122](pages/mains/mains_page_122.pdf)

Guardian of Parliamentary Privileges
1. Safeguards the rights, privileges, and independence of the House and its members.
2. Represents the House in all communications with the President and external authorities.
Role in Parliamentary Committees
1. Refers Bills to Parliamentary Committees for detailed examination.
2. Speaker nominates members to Committees and serves as ex-officio Chairperson of key bodies like the
Rules Committee and Business Advisory Committee.
Issues:
1. The Speaker combines both legislative leadership (presiding over sessions) and quasi-judicial
functions (anti-defection adjudication, privileges inquiries) creating conflict of interest.
2. Partisan Role and Political Bias - Eg. In Manipur and Maharashtra defection cases (2020-23), delay in
decisions benefited ruling coalitions.
3. Discretion in Disqualification under Tenth Schedule - Speaker is both judge and party member under
the Anti-Defection Law, creating a conflict of interest.
4. Suspension and Control of the House - Powers under Rule 374A give the Speaker unilateral authority to
suspend MPs for "grave disorder." Eg. 2023 mass suspension of 146 MPs
5. Speaker's certification under Article 110 is final and non-justiciable, enabling executive misuse. Eg.
Aadhaar Act (2016) passed as a Money Bill
6. Lack of Neutrality Safeguards - Unlike the UK, the Indian Speaker remains a party member and
contests elections on party tickets, compromising neutrality.
7. Article 122 - Judicial review of parliamentary proceedings is limited, allowing unchecked Speaker
discretion.
8. Decline in Parliamentary Deliberation - "railroading" Bills without adequate discussion (Eg. Farm Bills
2020 via voice vote).
9. Absence of Accountability Mechanisms - The Speaker is accountable only to the House majority,
which often coincides with the ruling party.
10.Increasing executive influence and declining impartiality have damaged the institutional credibility of

Money Bills
Article 110 of the Constitution of India outlines the definition of a Money Bill, stating that a bill is considered
a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with specific financial matters. These include:
1. The imposition, abolition, remission, alteration, or regulation of any tax.
2. The regulation of the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the GoI.
3. The custody of the Consolidated Fund or the Contingency Fund of India, the payment of money into or
the withdrawal of money from any such fund.
4. The appropriation of money out of the Consolidated Fund of India.
5. Declaring of any expenditure to be expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
6. The receipt of money on account of the Consolidated Fund of India or the public account of India or the
custody or issue of such money.
7. Any matter incidental to any of the matters specified above.
Exclusions from money bills as outlined in the Indian Constitution.
1. These include the imposition of fines, pecuniary penalties, fees for licenses or services, and local taxes
imposed by local authorities for local purposes.
2. These matters are not considered directly related to the central financial policies of the union
government.
Need:
1. Ensures Executive Speed: Allows the government to pass essential financial laws without the risk of
long-drawn delays in the Rajya Sabha. Eg. Finance Bill 2026
2. Reflects the principle that only the "House of the People" should have the final say on the people's
money.
3. Financial Stability: Prevents a "fiscal cliff" by ensuring that the Consolidated Fund of India is never
blocked by a political deadlock.
4. Exclusive Presidential Oversight: Requires prior recommendation of the President, ensuring the
executive and legislative wings are in sync.
5. Administrative Efficiency: Combines multiple fiscal measures into a single bill, reducing the legislative
burden on Parliament.
6. Constitutional Guardrails: Explicitly excludes "fines" or "fees for services" from being termed Money
Bills, preventing executive overreach.
Issues:
1. Bypassing the Rajya Sabha: Eg. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) and PMLA amendments
were passed via this route.
2. Legislative "Smuggling": Embedding non-financial provisions (like data privacy or tribunal reforms)
into a Finance Bill to fast-track them.
3. Role of Certifying Authority: Allegations have surfaced regarding the speaker's potentially biased role
due to the speaker's sole discretion in certifying a bill as a money bill.
4. Fiscal Mismanagement Risk: Limited scrutiny can lead to poorly considered financial policies.
5. Conflict with Article 117: The thin line between a "Money Bill" and a "Financial Bill (Type I)" is
frequently exploited to favor the former.

Joint Sitting of the Parliament
A Joint Sitting of Parliament is an extraordinary constitutional mechanism used to resolve a legislative
deadlock between the Lok Sabha (Lower House) and the Rajya Sabha (Upper House).
Constitutional Provisions (Article 108)
1. Summoning: The President of India summons the joint sitting after a deadlock arises.
2. Conditions for Deadlock: A joint sitting can be called if, after a bill is passed by one House and
transmitted to the other:
a. The bill is rejected by the other House.
b. The Houses have finally disagreed on the amendments to be made.
c. More than six months elapse from the date of reception without the bill being passed.
3. The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides. In their absence, the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha; if they are also
absent, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
4. Voting and Decision: The bill is passed by a simple majority of the total number of members of both
Houses present and voting.
5. Quorum: One-tenth of the total membership of both Houses.
